q: Professor Kim gives a definition of a program to keep. What is a program?
teach: From the lesson: written in advance, fetched and followed one by one.
teach2: From the lesson, in Professor Kim's words: 'A program is a set of instructions stored in memory, written in advance, that the processor fetches and follows one by one.' Another way: the clerk never invents his orders — a program is the orders, kept where he can fetch them.

q: Before a program can be written, something more basic has to exist. What is an algorithm?

q: In the lesson's worked program, the three prices are 4, 9, and 2 dollars. What total does the program finish with?
teach: From the lesson: the running total is kept in a variable called total.
teach2: From the lesson, in Professor Kim's words: 'Total is now 15. Position becomes three. Jump back. Is position at the end now? Yes, three is past the last price.' Another way: four plus nine plus two, added one at a time by the loop, lands on fifteen.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The loop adds each price to the running total in turn. (2) Four makes the total four, nine makes it thirteen, and two makes it fifteen. (3) The program finishes with the total 15.

q: What is a bug, in the lesson's exact sense of the word?
teach: From the lesson: the clerk executes a buggy instruction with perfect fidelity.
teach2: From the lesson, in Professor Kim's words: 'A bug is a mistake in the instructions, a place where the program says something other than what its writer meant.' Another way: the machine is rarely broken when a bug bites — the orders were wrong, and the clerk obeyed them beautifully.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The clerk does exactly what the program says, never what it meant. (2) So when the program says something other than what its writer meant, the result goes wrong. (3) That place in the instructions is a bug — a mistake in the instructions.

q: In the trace of the worked program, what is the running total after the second price has been added?

teach2: From the lesson, in Professor Kim's words: 'Add the price at position one, which is 9. Total is now 13. Position becomes two. Jump back.' Another way: the first price made the total four, and adding the second price, nine, brings it to thirteen.

q: In your own words, explain the stored program idea, and why it lets one and the same machine become a camera, a map, or an office.
teach: From the lesson: instructions are data — the beam the whole building rests on.
teach2: From the lesson, in Professor Kim's words: 'This is called the stored program idea, and it is what separates a computer from a calculator.' Another way to hold it: because the orders live in memory as changeable data, swapping the orders swaps the machine, while every wire stays exactly where it was.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The idea is that instructions are stored in memory as data, in the same bytes as the numbers. (2) Data can be replaced, so the stored instructions can be replaced. (3) In your own words: load different instructions and the same hardware becomes a different machine.
